title: Physical Quantities, Units and Measurement
seo_title: Secondary 3 Physics: Physical Quantities, Units and Measurement Worksheets (O-Level)
standard_code: O-Level Physics (6091): Physical Quantities, Units and Measurement
standard_text: Show understanding that all physical quantities consist of a numerical magnitude and a unit; recall the base quantities and their SI units (mass, length, time, current, temperature, amount of substance); use the prefixes nano, micro, milli, centi, kilo, mega and giga; distinguish between scalar and vector quantities and determine the resultant of two vectors; choose instruments to measure length and time with appropriate precision, and reduce random and systematic errors (summary of the Singapore-Cambridge O-Level Physics 6091 syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 3 O-Level Physics worksheets on physical quantities and units: SI base units, prefixes, scalars and vectors, resultant of two vectors, precision, significant figures and errors. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Vectors have size and direction; scalars have size only.
body_html:
How to think about it

Every physical quantity is a number with a unit.

  • SI base units: kg, m, s, A, K, mol. Prefixes: G 10⁹, M 10⁶, k 10³, c 10⁻², m 10⁻³, µ 10⁻⁶, n 10⁻⁹.
  • A vector (force, velocity, displacement) has direction. Two vectors at right angles: resultant = √(a² + b²).
  • Precision: metre rule 0.1 cm, vernier calipers 0.01 cm, micrometer screw gauge 0.01 mm.
  • Random errors: repeat and average. Systematic errors (such as a zero error): correct every reading. Time many oscillations and divide.
Example

Convert 450 mA into A.

milli = 10⁻³

450 × 10⁻³

Answer: 0.45 A

Example

Forces of 6 N and 8 N act at right angles. Resultant?

√(6² + 8²) = √100

Answer: 10 N

Example

20 oscillations take 32.0 s. Period?

32.0 ÷ 20

Answer: 1.60 s

Common mistakes

  • Thinking averaging removes a zero error. It only reduces random errors.
  • Adding two perpendicular vectors as numbers (3 N + 4 N = 7 N). Use Pythagoras.
  • Getting prefixes the wrong way round: 1 mA is 0.001 A, not 1000 A.
  • Calling mass or speed a vector. They have no direction.

faq.q: What are the SI base units?
faq.a: kilogram (mass), metre (length), second (time), ampere (current), kelvin (temperature) and mole (amount of substance).

faq.q: What is the difference between random and systematic errors?
faq.a: Random errors scatter readings above and below the true value and are reduced by averaging. Systematic errors shift every reading the same way and must be corrected.

faq.q: Why time many oscillations of a pendulum?
faq.a: Reaction time adds the same error to one long timing as to a short one, so timing 20 swings and dividing by 20 gives a more accurate period.

items.q: Which is the smallest time?
items.e: Nano is 10⁻⁹, the smallest of these prefixes.

items.q: What does every physical quantity consist of?
c: a numerical magnitude and a unit
items.e: For example 5.0 kg: 5.0 is the magnitude and kg is the unit.

items.q: What is the SI base unit of length?
Which prefix stands for 10<sup>−3</sup>?
The unit of density is kg/m³. Which base quantities is it made from?
items.e: Density = mass ÷ volume, and volume comes from length.

items.q: Convert 120 GW into W.
What is the SI unit of force, written in base units?
items.e: F = ma, so 1 N = 1 kg × 1 m/s².

Which prefix stands for 10<sup>6</sup>?
Which of these is a base quantity, not a derived quantity?
items.e: Speed, area and density are derived from base quantities.

Two forces of 8 N and 3 N act in opposite directions. What is the size of the resultant?
Is speed a scalar or a vector quantity?
items.e: A vector has magnitude and direction; a scalar has magnitude only. Speed is a scalar.

items.q: Two velocities of 3 m/s and 10 m/s act in opposite directions. What is the size of the resultant?

Is velocity a scalar or a vector quantity?
items.e: A vector has magnitude and direction; a scalar has magnitude only. Velocity is a vector.

items.q: Is friction a scalar or a vector quantity?
items.e: A vector has magnitude and direction; a scalar has magnitude only. Friction is a vector.

items.q: Which of these is a scalar quantity?
items.e: Speed has size only, no direction.

items.q: Is pressure a scalar or a vector quantity?
items.e: A vector has magnitude and direction; a scalar has magnitude only. Pressure is a scalar.

items.q: What is meant by a vector quantity?
c: a quantity with both magnitude and direction

items.q: Which of these is a vector quantity?
items.e: Velocity has a direction as well as a size.

items.q: Which is the largest length?
Which of these is a vector quantity?
items.e: Weight has a direction as well as a size.

Two velocities of 3 m/s and 4 m/s act at right angles to each other. What is the size of the resultant?
Which of these is a vector quantity?
items.e: Force has a direction as well as a size.

items.q: Why do you look straight down at a scale when you read it?
c: to see the scale more clearly
to make the reading more precise
items.e: Your eye must be level with the mark.

items.q: Which instrument has a precision of 0.01 cm (0.1 mm)?
A student measures the time for 20 swings of a pendulum three times: 28.6 s, 28.4 s and 28.5 s. What is the average value?
A student measures the time for a ball to roll down a ramp three times: 5.5 s, 5.3 s and 5.1 s. What is the average value?
Which instrument is most suitable for measuring the outside diameter of a test tube (about 1.6 cm)?
items.e: Precision: metre rule 0.1 cm, vernier calipers 0.01 cm, micrometer screw gauge 0.01 mm. Vernier calipers suits the outside diameter of a test tube (about 1.6 cm).

items.q: A student measures the time for a ball to roll down a ramp three times: 5.1 s, 5.0 s and 5.5 s. What is the average value?
Which instrument is most suitable for measuring the thickness of one sheet of paper?
items.e: Precision: metre rule 0.1 cm, vernier calipers 0.01 cm, micrometer screw gauge 0.01 mm. A micrometer screw gauge suits the thickness of one sheet of paper.

items.q: Which instrument is most suitable for measuring the depth of a test tube?
items.e: Precision: metre rule 0.1 cm, vernier calipers 0.01 cm, micrometer screw gauge 0.01 mm. Vernier calipers suits the depth of a test tube.

items.q: A student measures the time for a ball to roll down a ramp three times: 2.5 s, 2.7 s and 2.1 s. What is the average value?
How many significant figures are there in 0.00760?
items.e: Leading zeros do not count; zeros after the first non-zero digit and trailing zeros after a decimal point do count. 0.0076 has 3 significant figures.

items.e: Precision: metre rule 0.1 cm, vernier calipers 0.01 cm, micrometer screw gauge 0.01 mm. Vernier calipers suits the internal diameter of a beaker.

items.q: A student times 50 complete oscillations of a pendulum as 100 s. What is the period?
items.e: Period = total time ÷ number of oscillations = 100 ÷ 50 = 2 s.

items.q: A pendulum has a period of 2 s. How long do 50 complete oscillations take?
Which instrument has a precision of 0.01 mm?
Which instrument is most suitable for measuring the length of a football field?
items.e: Precision: metre rule 0.1 cm, vernier calipers 0.01 cm, micrometer screw gauge 0.01 mm. A measuring tape suits the length of a football field.

items.q: A pendulum has a period of 1.2 s. How long do 50 complete oscillations take?

A thermometer always reads 1 °C higher than the true temperature. What kind of error is this?
c: no error: the reading is exact
items.e: A systematic error shifts every reading the same way (fix it, e.g. correct the zero). A random error scatters readings (repeat and average).

items.q: A student times 20 complete oscillations of a pendulum as 16 s. What is the period?
items.e: Period = total time ÷ number of oscillations = 16 ÷ 20 = 0.8 s.

items.q: Why is the diameter of a wire measured at several places and averaged?
c: The wire may not be perfectly uniform, so the average is more accurate.
items.e: Repeat and average to reduce random errors.

items.e: A systematic error shifts every reading the same way (fix it, e.g. correct the zero). A random error scatters readings (repeat and average).

by repeating the measurement and taking the average
